items.title: Multicellular signaling in reverse cardiac remodeling revealed by integrated bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomics
items.summary: Heart failure results from maladaptive multicellular remodeling triggered by sustained biomechanical stress. Although mechanical unloading can promote reverse remodeling, recovery is frequently incomplete and its mechanistic basis remains unclear. Using a reversible murine pressure-overload model combined with bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomics, we demonstrate that reverse remodeling represents an actively maintained yet constrained multicellular state. Unloading improved cardiac function and partially restored extracellular matrix and metabolic programs, whereas inflammatory and mitochondrial dysfunction signatures persisted. Cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells largely re-established homeostatic transcriptional states, while fibroblasts retained activated programs that dominated residual pathology. Multicellular factor analysis delineated a reversible metabolic stress program and a persistent inflammatory-mitochondrial program coordinated across cardiac cell types.
items.author: Steier, M., Rivero-Garcia, I., Flores, R. O. R. et al.

items.title: Network modeling identifies vitamin B2 control of AIFM2 deficit-driven hepatocyte death in MASLD
items.summary: Drug discovery for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) remains difficult due to network effects. We developed MetaLiver, a public resource to identify druggable nodes within complex interactomes. It incorporates a MASLD-specific knowledge graph that improves bioactive compound contextualization while reducing computing time 18.8-fold. Layering progression-resolved bulk and hepatocyte-specific single-cell MASLD data onto this graph identified the vitamin B2-dependent flavoproteome (FlavProt) as an injury-sensitive network. Induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary human hepatocytes validated that flavin-cofactor replenishment mitigates FlavProt-dependent dysregulation, augmenting metabolic functions under cellular stress. Saturating flavin-cofactor availability blunted human immune cell activation. Clinically, a FlavProt expression score significantly correlated with poor outcomes in retrospectively stratified MASLD patients.
items.author: Weihs, J., Baldo, F., Cardinali, A. et al.

items.title: A dynamic displacement mechanism drives protein import into mitochondria
items.summary: Most mitochondrial proteins are produced in the cytosol and imported through the translocase of the outer mitochondrial membrane (TOM) to reach their final destination. Although this protein entry gate has been structurally characterized, it remains unclear how precursor proteins are handed off from the cytosolic receptor domains to the translocation pore. Here we show that the cytosolic domain of Tom22 - traditionally viewed as the central TOM receptor - acts not as a structured scaffold but as a largely disordered, flexible segment that plays an active role in precursor transfer. Atomic-level structural techniques and in vivo experiments identified a conserved short linear motif that forms a transient -helical element within this disordered domain.
items.author: Sucec, I., Guillerm, U., Schneider, J. et al.

items.title: From Network Topology to Parameterization: An Optimized Model of Endothelial Mechanobiology
items.summary: Endothelial cells integrate biomechanical and biochemical cues to regulate vascular function, which can be modeled using signaling networks. Yet, the extent to which their signaling behavior is determined by network topology versus reaction-specific parameterization remains unclear. We developed a continuous logic-based ordinary differential equation model of endothelial signaling containing 70 species and 123 regulatory reactions assembled from the literature. Model predictions were evaluated against 79 literature-defined responses to imposed wall stress, wall shear stress, hypoxia, or TNF. We first tested whether a single global parameter triplet (describing reaction weight, Hill coefficient, and half-maximal activation) could reproduce these observations. Investigator-selected global parameters reproduced 62/79 responses (78.48%).
items.author: Gueldner, P. H., Irons, L., Warren, J. L. et al.

items.title: Dynamic Hierarchical Interleaved Bloom Filter: An Updatable Index for Large-Scale Fast Sequence Search
items.summary: Motivation: A continued decrease in sequencing costs has facilitated the exponential increase in available sequencing data, with public databases like the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA) reaching well in the order of petabases. This has been the incentive to develop more scalable tools for common bioinformatics tasks. One such task is the approximate searching of short sequence patterns like genes or reads in reference data sets. In recent years, a variety of indexing data structures have been proposed for searching large sequencing databases. The state-of-the-art index, the Hierarchical Interleaved Bloom Filter (HIBF), was first-in-class to index one million samples.
items.author: Seiler, E., Willemsen, M., Piro, V. C. et al.

items.title: Ribonucleotide Reductase Inhibition Overcomes FLT3 Inhibitor Resistance in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
items.summary: Internal tandem duplication mutations in FLT3 (FLT3ITD) occur in approximately 30% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and are among the most common genetic alterations in this disease. FLT3ITD is a major driver of AML and associated with poor clinical outcomes. Although FLT3 inhibitors (FLT3is) have significantly improved outcomes for patients with FLT3ITD+ AML, acquired resistance remains a major barrier to durable clinical benefit. Reactivation of RAS/MAPK signaling, often driven by activating NRAS mutations, is a major mechanism of FLT3i resistance in AML; however, effective strategies to overcome this resistance remain lacking. Here, we identify ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) as a critical therapeutic vulnerability in NRAS-driven FLT3i-resistant FLT3ITD+ AML.
items.author: Tian, Z., Zhang, H., Chatla, S. et al.

items.title: Interpersonal alignment in infra-slow EEG rhythms and bodily signals anticipates mutual recognition
items.summary: Across multiple timescales, neural rhythms coordinate cognitive and physiological processes. Slower rhythms are increasingly recognised as the scale at which autonomic and interoceptive processes are folded into ongoing cognition, a brain&body view of allostatic regulation that is particularly relevant to social interaction. Examining these slow components of the electroencephalogram (EEG) during real-time interaction remains challenging. Here, we recorded infra-slow EEG alongside respiratory, cardiac and skin conductance signals during the perceptual crossing experiment, a social interaction and EEG hyperscanning paradigm. We assessed interpersonal alignment by contrasting trials in which dyads achieved mutual recognition with trials in which they did not, which separates genuine social alignment or recognition from a shared anticipatory context.
items.author: Gravel, N., Guendelman, S., Vidaurre, D.

items.title: Spatiospectral signatures of stomach-brain synchrony
items.summary: While cognitive neuroscience has increasingly recognized the brain-body connection, the temporal dynamics of how the stomach's intrinsic rhythm (~0.05 Hz) modulates human neural activity remain poorly understood. Leveraging high-resolution magneto- encephalography (MEG) and novel high-density electrogastrography (EGG), we provide the first comprehensive spatiotemporal mapping of human gastric-brain coupling at rest. Our circular-linear correlation approach revealed widespread, broadband phase-amplitude coupling between the gastric rhythm and spontaneous cortical oscillations across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Using nonnegative matrix factorization, we identified distinct spatiospectral fingerprints that significantly overlap with the known fMRI-based gastric resting-state network. Functional connectivity analyses based on multivariate Granger causality further showed that these modulation patterns extend to a gastric influence on frequency-specific, directed communication between network components.
items.author: Berther, T., Saltafossi, M., Fehring, J. et al.

items.title: Spreading depolarization, not seizure activity, drives immediate early gene expression in mouse cortex after electroconvulsive stimulation
items.summary: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a highly effective treatment for several psychiatric disorders, though its biological mechanisms remain unclear. ECT's therapeutic action has traditionally been attributed to the generalized seizure it induces. However, this view is challenged by the recent finding that electroconvulsive stimulation (ECS) can trigger a spreading depolarization (SD) in cortex. Because SD drives massive molecular changes, including expression of the plasticity-related immediate early gene Fos, we hypothesized that SD could be a key mediator of ECT's plasticity-inducing effects. We recorded the neuronal response to ECS in mouse dorsal cortex and observed similar activity to that of patients undergoing ECT.
items.author: Ladret, H. J., Lupori, L., Sieni, L. et al.

items.title: Decoding Articulatory and Phonetic Features: Somatotopic and Sensorimotor Representations in Native and Non-native Consonant Perception
items.summary: Speech perception relies on the integration of auditory and articulatory information, yet the precise role of motor regions remains debated. We combined fMRI with multivariate pattern analyses (MVPA) and behavioral measures to investigate cortical representations of native French and non-native Mandarin consonant perception under clear and noisy conditions. Cross-modal classification analysis showed that articulator-specific features of perceived degraded native bilabial and dental consonants are mapped somatotopically in right lip and tongue motor areas, which are also engaged in consonant production. These representations may support consonant categorization by compensating for degraded auditory input. Representational similarity analysis further revealed that a network encompassing bilateral temporal auditory and frontal motor regions encodes phonetic features, including place and manner of articulation, for both native and non-native consonants.
items.author: Tseng, T., Thibault, S., Krzonowski, J. et al.

items.title: Peripheral detection of viruses shapes brain immunity and behavior in zebrafish
items.summary: Olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) are constantly exposed to pathogens, including viruses. However, serious brain infection via the olfactory route rarely occurs. When OSNs detect a virus, they coordinate local antiviral immune responses to stop virus progression to the brain. Despite effective immune control in the olfactory periphery, pathogen-triggered neuronal signals reach the CNS via the olfactory bulb (OB). We hypothesized that neuronal detection of a virus by OSNs initiates neuroimmune responses in the OB that prevent pathogen invasion. Using zebrafish (Danio rerio) as a model, we demonstrate viral-specific neuronal activation of OSNs projecting into the OB, indicating that OSNs are electrically activated by viruses.
items.author: Kraus, A., Garcia, B., Ma, J. et al.

items.title: The bile acid receptor TGR5 is a modulator of the bone marrow microenvironment
items.summary: The gut is an emerging regulator of bone marrow (BM) hematopoiesis, with several molecules involved in this communication. Among them, bile acids (BAs) act as a relay between the microbiota and the rest of the body by activating specific receptors, including Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5). Although TGR5 has potent regulatory effects in immune cells, its role in the BM remains unclear. Here, we show that TGR5 is expressed across hematopoietic populations, including hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. While TGR5 deficiency did not affect steady-state hematopoiesis, it mildly impaired cell-autonomous short-term hematopoietic reconstitution. In contrast, TGR5 deletion altered the BM microenvironment.
items.author: Alonso-Calleja, A., Perino, A., Schyrr, F. et al.

items.title: Identification of a somatic H3K23me3 methyltransferase SET-19 in C. elegans
items.summary: Histone methylation plays essential roles in modulating chromatin organization and gene expression. H3K23 methylation is a conserved histone modification, yet its biological roles and the enzymes responsible for its deposition remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the loss of set-19 leads to a pronounced reduction in H3K23 methylation in C. elegans, as revealed by quantitative mass spectrometry, western blotting, and immunofluorescence staining. In vitro biochemical assays show that recombinant SET-19 proteins purified from E. coli directly catalyze H3K23 methylation. Genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation assays reveal that H3K23me3 is enriched at heterochromatic regions and that loss of set-19 alters H3K23me3 levels, accompanied by derepression of a subset of genes.
items.author: Xu, M., Fan, Z., Yan, C. et al.

items.title: Can Folding Models Tell Binders from Bluffers? Evidence from POISK: The Patent-Derived Antibody Dataset
items.summary: Structure prediction models are increasingly deployed as zero-shot digital screens in antibody design, operating under the assumption that high folding confidence implies true binding. However, rigorous validation of this premise has been limited by small test sets, narrow target diversity, and the risk of data leakage from training-adjacent structures. Here we introduce POISK: Patent-extracted Organization of Immunoglobulin Sequence Knowledge, a large-scale dataset derived from the US patent literature, comprising 89074 antibody-antigen records extracted from 10110 patents using an LLM-based pipeline. From this resource, we curate a balanced benchmark set of 22494 complexes: 11247 patent-validated binders without a known resolved structure paired with putative non-binders constructed from sequence-similar human repertoire antibodies.
items.author: Tupikina, D., Roncoli, A., Bujotzek, A. et al.

items.title: CellChat Hotspot: A Targeted Approach to Cell Cell Communication Analysis With Spatial transcriptomics Validation.
items.summary: Abstract. In recent years, single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA seq) has enabled the investigation of intercellular communication through Cell Cell Communication (CCC) tools such as CellChat. Despite their potential, these approaches remain challenging to interpret, particularly when global analyses generate complex interaction networks that may include biologically irrelevant signals. To address this limitation, we developed a framework termed CellChat Hotspot, designed to improve the biological interpretability of inferred communication networks. This approach integrates gene set enrichment analysis with a context driven filtering strategy, selecting both genes and cells based on their functional relevance prior to communication inference. Applied to stage II colon cancer data, CellChat Hotspot enabled the identification of condition-specific interaction patterns associated with recurrence.
items.author: Monaco, D., Dioguardi, M., Dipalma, M. et al.

items.title: Combined EZH1/2 and DNMT inhibition overcomes transcriptional barriers imposed by drug-induced epigenetic plasticity in colorectal cancer cells
items.summary: Abnormal DNA methylation patterning is a defining epigenetic hallmark of human cancers and is therapeutically targetable with DNA methyltransferase inhibitors (DNMTi's). However, epigenetic plasticity involving Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2)-dependent H3K27 methylation can constrain transcriptional responses to DNMTi's and may contribute to their limited activity in solid tumors. Here, we compare pharmacologic strategies targeting EZH1 and EZH2 in combination with DNMT inhibition in colorectal cancer (CRC) cells and define the molecular features that distinguish EZH2-selective from dual EZH1/2 inhibition. We find that dual EZH1/2 inhibition produces more robust transcriptional activation when combined with DNMT inhibition and more extensive depletion of H3K27 methylation states than EZH2-selective inhibition.
items.author: Chomiak, A. A., Wiseman, A. K., Hrit, J. A. et al.

items.title: Activation of perivascular thermogenic fat improves aortic stenosis
items.summary: Aim: Aortic stenosis (AS) is a common condition with exponential increases in incidence in aging populations. Perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) forms the outer layer of the aortic wall and has - especially in the thoracic area - characteristics of thermogenic adipose tissue, which dissipates energy and releases endocrine factors. Here, we set out to investigate the role of thermogenic PVAT in AS. Methods and results: We studied the role of (PVAT) in the development of AS in a murine model of AS. To specifically delineate the role of PVAT activity in AS, we used a pharmacological {beta}3-adrenergic agonist as well as cold exposure in combination with a genetic mouse model with deficient PVAT development.
items.author: Hildebrand, S., Wunderling, K., Siwik-Rog, Z. et al.

items.title: Mathematical Modeling of the Canonical Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor Pathway in murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages
items.summary: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is a ligand-activated transcription factor involved in xenobiotic sensing, as well as development, immunity, and tissue homeostasis. AhR signaling proceeds through a canonical and a non-canonical branch. It remains unclear which biochemical steps of the canonical pathway are responsible for distinct ligand specific transcriptional responses. Here, we developed a mechanistic ordinary differential equation model of the canonical AhR pathway in murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages. We calibrated it to time-resolved qPCR measurements of Cyp1a1 and Ahrr mRNA in mouse bone-marrow-derived macrophages exposed to three structurally diverse, environmentally relevant ligands with known immunomodulatory activity: 3-methylcholanthrene, indolo[3,2-]carbazole and bisphenol A.
items.author: Wieland, V., Blum, T., Iriady, I. et al.

items.title: Acute FMR1 reduction alters cellular and circuit properties in human cortex
items.summary: Transcriptional silencing of FMR1 results in Fragile X syndrome (FXS), the leading inherited cause of intellectual disability (ID) and autism. Although the impact of FMR1 reduction on cortical function has been studied using the Fmr1-/y mouse model, mechanistic insights from the human brain are lacking. Here we show that acute FMR1 reduction in ex vivo human cortical slices induces transcriptomic changes that are concordant with those observed in FXS patient cortex, identifying many targets not altered in the Fmr1-/y mouse model. Consistent with changes in ion channel expression specifically in human tissue, FMR1 reduction drives increased intrinsic excitability of deep-layer pyramidal neurons and network-level population bursts observed with two-photon calcium imaging.
items.author: Singh, A., Abbaspoor, S., Chung, L. et al.

items.title: Distinct contemplative traditions share a common EEG complexity signature
items.summary: Meditation encompasses diverse practices that train attention inward, unlike externally oriented task states. Which brain-activity features are shared across contemplative practices, which accompany long-term training, and which are tradition-specific remains unclear. We leveraged electroencephalography data from 226 participants: advanced meditators of four contemplative traditions and non-meditating controls. We developed a neurodynamic profiling approach spanning 21 features across four feature families: oscillatory, aperiodic, complexity and timescale. Using extensive machine learning, we found that meditation and task states were reliably separable, driven by a large, uniform drop in complexity during meditation. Meditators differed from controls primarily in timescale dynamics. Traditions exhibited distinct signatures in all feature families except complexity, and meditators neurodynamic profiles identified the contemplative tradition they practiced.
items.author: Shrimali, P., Sasidharan, A., Malipeddi, S. et al.

items.title: Loss of riboflavin biosynthesis leads to accumulation of select aromatic amino acids and loss of infectivity in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
items.summary: Riboflavin biosynthesis is required for in vitro survival of the human pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). However, despite the lack of a known transporter, growth can be rescued by exogenous riboflavin. The riboflavin biosynthesis pathway is also predicted essential in vivo, but whether riboflavin levels available in the host can support survival has not been directly tested. Here we constructed a set of inducible CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) knockdown and targeted gene deletion strains for known riboflavin biosynthesis genes (ribA2, ribG, ribH, ribC) as tools to characterize riboflavin requirements, uptake, and metabolite changes and to assess in vivo essentiality. We found that riboflavin, but not flavin adenine dinucleotide or flavin mononucleotide, rescued auxotrophy for all strains tested.
items.author: Jaisinghani, N., Arasappan, A., Pradhan, A. et al.

items.title: Measuring satellite arrays of the human Y chromosome from sequencing reads
items.summary: Human Y chromosome satellites vary widely but remain difficult to measure in large cohorts. We developed Yruler, which uses pangenome assemblies to measure satellite lengths, composition and Y dosage from sequencing reads without alignment. Across cohorts, we find lineage-associated differences in centromere and non-centromeric array length, and show that heterochromatin components vary unequally within lineages. Yruler enables population-scale studies of how Y satellite variation relates to health and disease.
items.author: Ortigas-Vasquez, A., Guarracino, A.

items.title: CNVSIM: an interpretable cross-study copy-number reference atlas for cancer subtyping
items.summary: Genome-wide copy-number variation (CNV) profiles provide a representation of structural changes in cancer genomes, but interpreting new profiles with respect to their underlying biology remains challenging. We developed CNVSIM, which organizes CNV profiles into root-specific reference spaces and defines subtypes with chromosome-scale and gene-level signatures. Applied to the Progenetix dataset, CNVSIM established 112 CNV-defined subtypes across 19 cancer roots, supported by 155,881 neoplastic analyses from diverse studies and assay platforms. In the context of diagnostic concepts, these subtypes distinguish genomic architectures and reveal associated differences in somatic mutation patterns, with selected associations supported across cohorts. In practice, CNVSIM enables new profiles to be projected onto the established reference and linked to corresponding reference analyses.
items.author: YU, J., Bardet-Trouilloud, J., Jaeger, S. et al.

items.title: pH-driven dynamics and mechanisms of LNP-mediated siRNA delivery
items.summary: We present a comprehensive analysis of a clinically relevant DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3)-based lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation that exhibits strong short interfering RNA (siRNA, ~21 nt) delivery and potent inhibition of targeted RNAs. Using a combination of coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, we characterize the pH-dependent structure of both unloaded and siRNA-loaded LNPs, elucidate the mechanism of siRNA encapsulation, and use these models to propose a plausible mechanism of endosomal escape. Consistent with prior experimental and computational studies, our simulations reproduce an inverted-hexagonal-type morphology in a ~70 nm siRNA-loaded LNPs. For the smaller LNPs mimetics, with only one siRNA sequence, we observe a similar hydrated core as observed in the larger 70 nm LNP model.
items.author: Hossain, K. A., Valerio, M., Medina, P. et al.

items.title: A general method for bootstrapping dense 3D segmentations from sparse 2D annotations
items.summary: Volumetric electron microscopy (vEM) provides unparalleled insight into cellular architecture, transforming our understanding of fundamental biological processes. Precise quantification of volumetric bioimaging data requires 3D instance segmentation, but the time and cost of manual ground-truth annotation present a major bottleneck for training accurate machine learning models. Our lightweight two-stage method generates complete 3D instance segmentations from sparse 2D annotations. A 2D network predicts dense boundaries on every section from minimal 2D labels. A 3D network pre- trained on synthetic data infers connectivity between sections. Across the imaging modalities and biological structures tested, our method generates base segmentations with minutes of human effort per volume.
items.author: Thiyagarajan, V. V., Sheridan, A., Harris, K. M. et al.

items.title: Synaptic pruning, myelination and the emergence of psychiatric disorders in late adolescence
items.summary: Adolescence is an important developmental period during which there are diverse changes in the brain and behavior. Goal-directed behaviors, including working memory, response inhibition, and reinforcement learning, improve during adolescence. At the same time there is substantial pruning of excitatory connections in prefrontal cortex and ongoing myelination of axons, which likely underlie these improvements in behavior. However, psychiatric disorders also become increasingly prevalent in late adolescence. In this study, we develop computational models that suggest a hypothesis for how ongoing changes in the brain can give rise to the increased prevalence of psychiatric disorders including depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), schizophrenia and substance use disorders (SUDs).
items.author: Averbeck, B. B., Brunel, N.

items.title: Assessing multi-eGO Predictions of PDZ2-Peptide Binding across Mutations
items.summary: Accurately predicting how mutations alter protein-peptide binding remains challenging for molecular simulations because both conformational sampling and binding kinetics are computationally demanding. Here, we investigate whether multi-eGO, a hybrid transferable/structure-based atomistic-resolution model previously developed and validated for protein-small molecule interactions, can be transferred to protein-peptide binding. Using the PDZ2 domain of protein tyrosine phosphatase basophil-like in complex with the peptide EQVTAV as a benchmark, we show that multi-eGO, calibrated on explicit-solvent simulations of the complex, predicts the equilibrium dissociation constant of the complex within the expected uncertainty, although binding and unbinding are both accelerated by several orders of magnitude. We then introduce conservative mutations in PDZ2 and in the peptide without additional training for each mutant.
items.author: Ardizzone, C., Stegani, B., Bacic Toplek, F. et al.

items.title: Network modularity reveals context and state-dependent reorganization of time-varying functional connectivity in single-cell resolved neural activity recordings
items.summary: An important goal of neuroscience is to understand how biological neural networks organize activity at multiple scales to enable complex information processing and behavioral output. To address this challenge, large-scale neural activity datasets with increased resolution and wider coverage have become more prevalent across many model systems. However, bridging the gap in scale between changes in pairwise functional connectivity between neurons and changes in brain-wide organization of activity remains a key challenge. In this work, we demonstrate application of modularity-based community detection and network modularity to single-cell resolved recordings, for the first time, as a method to summarize complex changes in time-varying functional connectivity, facilitating comparisons across multiple time windows, recordings, and conditions.
items.author: Moon, S., Liang, J., Lee, H. J. et al.

items.title: Reactive and predictive processes during unpredictable driving collisions in virtual reality: an exploratory immersive study with multimodal neurophysiological monitoring
items.summary: Anticipatory neurophysiological activity before unpredictable emotional events has been reported for decades, but the effects are small, difficult to replicate, and obtained almost exclusively in stripped-down laboratory paradigms. Whether they reflect genuine predictive processes or methodological artifacts remains debated; one rarely tested possibility is that such settings mute it. We examined anticipation in an immersive virtual reality (VR) driving simulation whose collision outcomes were assigned by a quantum random number generator, while EEG, photoplethysmography (PPG), EMG, EOG and inertial (IMU) signals were recorded from a single wireless dry-electrode headset built into the VR display. Sixteen participants passively observed 120 driving sequences ending in a collision or no collision.
items.author: Cannard, C., Yesilbas, D.

items.title: Immersive display systems for simulating natural vision
items.summary: Vision is traditionally studied using simplified stimuli presented briefly near the center of a flat display while subjects maintain visual fixation. This paradigm contrasts sharply with real-world vision, which is immersive, dynamic and strongly influenced by self-initiated actions. Traditional approaches have allowed researchers to systematically study the neural encoding of visual features and the influence of cognitive operations such as attention. However, other methods are needed to study more holistic and first-person perspectives on vision, such as those related to physical space, continuous time, and self-movement. To enable the study of these and other aspects of real-world vision, we developed hemispherical ("dome") display systems for macaque visual neuroscience.
items.author: Katti, H., Murphy, A. P., Helde, M. et al.

items.title: Evaluating Markovian Models for Maritime Data Fusion
items.summary: Monitoring maritime security is difficult due to domain complexity, prompting the use of Automatic Identification System data combined with space-based radio frequency observations. This study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model to align individual radio frequency detections with Automatic Identification System trajectories, accounting for temporal and spatial details. Evaluated on National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data against baseline approaches, the method achieves notable precision and area-under-curve scores for detecting unflagged vessels. While a log-odds variant improves performance, a simpler time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline maintains higher overall accuracy.
items.author: Daniel Grimm, Kyra Jongman, Renato Cordeiro Ferreira et al.
items.original_title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
items.original_summary: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies.

items.title: FETTUCCINE Brings Brain-to-Text Decoding to Mobile Devices
items.summary: Researchers have introduced FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end framework designed to decode neural activity during attempted speech into text using automatic speech recognition models. Traditional brain-to-text systems rely on compute-intensive language modeling stacks that cause high and variable latencies, hindering real-world communication. FETTUCCINE addresses these issues by achieving low word error rates while running efficiently on commercial mobile devices. When tested on public data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, the framework achieved a word error rate as low as 4.39 percent and reached up to 370 times real-time throughput on mobile hardware. Furthermore, the models can be fine-tuned to adapt to daily neural changes and allow for the localization of relevant neural features.
items.author: Jonathan D. McCart, Pranav I. Deevi, Mehdi Azabou et al.
items.original_title: FETTUCCINE: Fast and efficient brain-to-text decoding on mobile devices
items.original_summary: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices.

items.title: Training Open-Weight Reasoning Models for Native Robot Control in Simulation
items.summary: Robot-use agents typically achieve strong performance only through proprietary frontier models, leaving open-weight models far less capable. To bridge this gap, researchers trained an open-weight 27B reasoning model entirely in simulation using reinforcement learning without human demonstrations. By developing a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics, the model learned to observe environments, reason through chains of thought, and generate end-effector poses natively. Evaluated on real dual-arm robots and benchmark tasks like LIBERO, the simulated training enabled the model to succeed across unseen setups and tasks, drastically improving success rates compared to base models while preserving core reasoning and coding capabilities.
items.author: Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Junxian Guo et al.
items.original_title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
items.original_summary: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use.

items.title: Self-Supervised Human Movement Modeling via Bidirectional Latent Autoregression
items.summary: Understanding human movement from 3D pose sequences typically relies on self-supervised methods dependent on artificial assumptions and heuristic hyperparameters. To overcome these limitations, researchers proposed BAL, a framework that uses the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior as intrinsic supervision. Instead of predicting precise joint configurations, BAL autoregressively forecasts movements within a semantically abstract latent space in both forward and backward directions. This bidirectional approach uses past and future context while avoiding representation collapse by splitting prediction targets into global semantic components and local context-independent movement components. Experiments confirm that BAL improves performance across various motion capture, forecasting, and interpolation tasks.
items.author: Genki Kinoshita, Ko Nishino
items.original_title: BAL: Bidirectional Autoregression in Latent Space for Learning Human Movement Representations
items.original_summary: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference.
items.ai_title: Self-Supervised Human Movement Modeling via Bidirectional Latent Autoregression
items.ai_summary: Understanding human movement from 3D pose sequences typically relies on self-supervised methods dependent on artificial assumptions and heuristic hyperparameters. To overcome these limitations, researchers proposed BAL, a framework that uses the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior as intrinsic supervision. Instead of predicting precise joint configurations, BAL autoregressively forecasts movements within a semantically abstract latent space in both forward and backward directions. This bidirectional approach uses past and future context while avoiding representation collapse by splitting prediction targets into global semantic components and local context-independent movement components. Experiments confirm that BAL improves performance across various motion capture, forecasting, and interpolation tasks.

items.title: Reconstructing Dynamical Dark Energy and Gravity from Observational Data
items.summary: Recent cosmological data has prompted renewed interest in whether deviations from standard cosmic expansion history involve changes in gravitational dynamics. Researchers performed a joint, non-parametric reconstruction of effective dark energy density alongside gravitational response functions using data from the Cosmic Microwave Background, baryon acoustic oscillations, supernovae, and large-scale structures. The analysis revealed a persistent maximum in effective dark energy density at redshifts between 0.5 and 0.7, indicating a crossing of the effective phantom divide. Although background expansion history shows clear departures from standard models, gravitational response functions remain less constrained, highlighting areas for future Stage IV cosmological surveys to investigate.
items.author: Maria Luisa Gallavotti, Alessandra Silvestri
items.original_title: Reconstruction of Dynamical Dark Energy and Gravity from latest cosmological data
items.original_summary: Recent cosmological observations have renewed interest in non-standard late-time evolution. We investigate whether departures from the standard expansion history are accompanied by modifications of gravitational dynamics through a joint, non-parametric reconstruction of the effective dark energy density, $Ω_{\rm X}(a)$, and the gravitational response functions $μ(a)$ and $Σ(a)$. Combining CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+, and large scale structure observations, including DES Year 3 $6\times2$pt data, we perform reconstructions with and without a theory motivated correlation prior derived from stable Horndeski models. We find a persistent maximum in $Ω_{\rm X}$ at $z\simeq0.5$--$0.7$, corresponding to a crossing of the effective phantom divide. This feature is already present in the CMB+BAO combination and remains robust when modifications to clustering and lensing are allowed.

items.title: Investigating the Evolution and Clustering Properties of Dark Energy
items.summary: Recent cosmological findings have spurred investigations into whether dynamical dark energy and shifts in cosmic expansion are accompanied by modified gravitational dynamics. Scientists conducted a joint, non-parametric reconstruction using data from the Cosmic Microwave Background, baryon acoustic oscillations, and supernovae, alongside large-scale structure surveys. The study identified a broad peak in effective dark energy density around redshifts 0.6 to 0.7, accompanied by minor low-redshift enhancements in gravitational responses. However, a combined covariance-mode analysis revealed that current data primarily constrain background expansion tightly, while the gravitational clustering sector remains less certain. Consequently, upcoming Stage-IV surveys will be required to confirm whether these low-redshift anomalies share a common physical origin.
items.author: Maria Luisa Gallavotti, Alessandra Silvestri
items.original_title: Does Dark Energy Evolve $\textit{and}$ Cluster?

items.title: Connecting Pure Spinors to Superspace Superfields
items.summary: This study links the pure spinor formalism with the superspace description of constrained superfields and gauge multiplets, primarily focusing on abelian two-dimensional N=(2,2) supersymmetry alongside three- and four-dimensional N=1 examples. By providing an explicit module over the supertranslation Chevalley-Eilenberg algebra for each multiplet, the work matches reconstructions with known superfields. First-order constraints derive from modules supported on linear subspaces of the nilpotence variety, while higher-order constraints emerge from Yoneda products. Requiring connections to act on matter and its conjugate restricts curvatures, yielding ordinary, twisted, and semichiral vector multiplets and their field strengths.
items.author: Ondrej Hulik, Raphael Senghaas
items.original_title: From pure spinor modules to superspace superfields
items.original_summary: We relate the pure spinor formalism to the superspace description of constrained superfields and gauge multiplets, mainly for abelian two-dimensional N=(2,2) supersymmetry, with three- and four-dimensional N=1 examples for comparison. For each multiplet we give an explicit module over the supertranslation Chevalley-Eilenberg algebra and match its reconstruction with the known superfields. First-order constraints come from modules supported on linear subspaces of the nilpotence variety, and higher-order ones, such as the complex-linear constraint, from Yoneda products of their Ext classes. Requiring a connection to act on given matter and its conjugate restricts its curvature, which yields the ordinary, twisted and semichiral vector multiplets with their field strengths.

items.title: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers via WEIGHTBENCH
items.summary: Recent advancements demonstrate that large language models can directly read, fix, and write neural network parameters without gradient descent, a paradigm known as Weight-Space Programming. To systematically evaluate this capability, researchers introduced WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark consisting of 42 tasks across five tracks, including reading, fixing, writing weights, recognizing impossible edits, and data-free compression. Tested models ranged from small control policies to 7-billion parameter language models. Experimental results reveal that while frontier agents can read small networks and write control policies without executing them, they struggle with patching large language models, data-free compression, and distinguishing complex edits.
items.author: Aayush Marasini, Barsat Khadka, Nick Rahimi
items.original_title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
items.original_summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models.

items.title: Real-Time Simulation of Scattering and Wave Packet Preparation in Scalar Field Theory
items.summary: Probing real-time dynamics in quantum field theory requires precise asymptotic incoming states. Researchers optimize a superposition of single particle momentum eigenstates and a single interpolating operator via eigenvalue problems to maximize preparation fidelity from the interacting vacuum. This creates a localized excitation, allowing weighted sums over lattice sites to prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent. Relative phases are calibrated using Lorentz symmetry to ensure the correct continuum limit. Analysis shows that single particle wave packet propagation creates oscillatory Airy distortions from saddle point interference at matching group velocities. These oscillations weaken near the continuum limit. Additionally, two-particle scattering simulations in scalar field theory reveal artificial inelasticity driven by coarse digitization or sampling deviations, allowing researchers to control these artifacts.
items.author: Boyu Gao, Natalie Klco
items.original_title: Real-time simulation of scattering in $φ^4$ theory: localized excitation, scalable wave packet preparation, and peak-generating artifacts
items.original_summary: Probing real-time dynamics is essential for understanding non-perturbative scattering and interactions in quantum field theory. A common challenge in real-time simulation is preparing accurate asymptotic incoming states. Through efficiently solvable eigenvalue problems, we jointly optimize a superposition of single particle momentum eigenstates and a single site interpolating operator to maximize preparation fidelity from the interacting vacuum. This leads to a localized excitation in the interacting theory analogous to a position eigenstate. Weighted sums of the resulting interpolating operator over lattice sites prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent. To ensure that this construction produces the correct continuum limit, relative phases among single particle momentum eigenstates in this superposition are calibrated using a relation derived from Lorentz symmetry.

items.title: Modeling Continuum Robot Friction Using Complementarity Constraints
items.summary: Accurate friction modeling is critical for motion control in continuum robots, yet traditional methods only predict internal friction restricted by the Coulomb friction cone, missing static friction and motion hysteresis. To address this, researchers proposed a new friction model utilizing complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption. This approach effectively predicts static friction, sliding friction, hysteresis behavior, and robot deformation caused by environmental interactions. The model operates efficiently in real time to meet robotic computing demands. Experimental validation on a tendon-driven continuum robot demonstrated that incorporating this friction model successfully reduced the maximum tip position error significantly compared to a frictionless model.
items.author: Jia Shen, Junhyoung Ha, Yue Chen
items.original_title: Modeling the Frictional Contact of Continuum Robots with Environments through Linear Complementarity Problem
items.original_summary: Accurate friction modeling in continuum robots is essential for precise motion control and path planning. However, current approaches make predictions only for the mechanism's internal friction that is limited by the boundary forces of the Coulomb friction cone, which fail to characterize the static friction and motion hysteresis. In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption. This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots.

items.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Demonstrations accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning, but extending this to multi-agent settings is difficult because teleoperating multiple agents simultaneously is challenging. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning allows a single demonstrator to control one agent at a time while others follow current policies, though performance remains capped by demonstration quality. To overcome this, researchers introduced Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, extending imitation bootstrapping to cooperative teams using Round-Robin Behavior Cloning. At each step, agents receive action proposals from both imitation and reinforcement learning policies, which an ensemble of centralized critics evaluates. A gated penalty regularizes the reinforcement learning policy toward the imitation policy only when favored by critics. Across benchmarks, this framework surpassed its imitation policies faster than baseline methods and occasionally exceeded the human demonstrator.
items.author: Tony H. Zhang, Connor Mattson, Daniel S. Brown
items.original_title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.original_summary: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies.

items.title: Elliptic Schedules and Zoloflow Sampling for Generative Models
items.summary: Generative modeling using stochastic interpolants requires choosing an interpolant schedule and a probability-flow ODE discretization. A new framework uses complexified ODE trajectory analyticity to design joint schedules and discretizations via conformal mapping. This approach yields variance-preserving elliptic schedules parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Combined with a tailored discretization, it produces Zoloflow, a sampling algorithm related to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. The method incorporates the target distribution's condition number and matches classical trigonometric schedules in specific limits. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality. For log-concave cases, the elliptic schedule allows efficient sampling with low Wasserstein error. Empirical evaluations on synthetic benchmarks and image generation datasets demonstrate the performance of these elliptic schedules against alternatives.
items.author: Cole Becker, Taylan Kargin, Kimia Hassibi et al.
items.original_title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
items.original_summary: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants.

items.title: Geometric Quantization and Giant Gravitons in Gauge Theories
items.summary: Researchers describe a reorganization of gauge-invariant operators in free or twisted U(N) gauge theories into single-trace and determinant operators using open loop equations. This reorganization provides a holographic interpretation where finite-N states are reproduced by applying N-independent gauge constraints to closed strings Fock space combined with the geometric quantization of Giant Graviton D-brane moduli spaces, utilizing a quantization parameter of N inverse. The moduli space of these D-branes arises from tachyon condensation of auxiliary D-brane and anti-D-brane pairs that are Koszul dual to the original gauge theory system. Furthermore, open loop equations are imposed using BRST complexes, whose homology conjecturally recovers the finite-N BPS Hilbert space in the large auxiliary rank limit, categorifying Murthy's Giant Graviton Expansion.
items.author: Kasia Budzik, Davide Gaiotto
items.original_title: Geometric Quantization of the Giant Graviton Master Moduli Space
items.original_summary: We describe a remarkable reorganization of the space of gauge invariant operators of free or twisted $U(N)$ gauge theories as combinations of single-trace and determinant operators modulo certain "open loop equations". The reorganization has a transparent holographic interpretation, describing how states at finite $N$ can be reproduced by imposing certain $N$-independent gauge constraints on the combination of the closed strings Fock space and a geometric quantization of the moduli space of Giant Graviton D-branes, with quantization parameter $N^{-1}$. The moduli space of Giant Graviton D-branes is reproduced from tachyon condensation of auxiliary D-brane/anti-D-brane pairs which are "Koszul dual" to the D-brane system which supports the original gauge theory.

items.title: Mathematical Theory Explains Finite Intelligence in Infinite Environments
items.summary: Information systems often need to learn before knowing what specific tasks they will encounter. Finite representations can succeed without recording an entire infinite environment if the tasks share collective structure. This paper formalizes this through future-task information, representing the minimum retained data required to preserve decision value. Under specific compactness conditions, every retained representation has a calibrated replacement based on a joint decision-regret state, preserving task regrets without increasing information. The resulting information-regret curve functions as an operational coding rate. Exact boundaries govern finite preservation, including weak-star closure and singular mass source-evidence laws. Collective structure dictates information requirements beyond individual question difficulty, revealing how nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish information preservation from efficient discovery and use in complex environments.
items.author: Mojtaba Soltanalian
items.original_title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
items.original_summary: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate.

items.title: ModHarness-RL: Evolving Harnesses for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning typically relies on a static, hand-written harness that controls what model interactions and guidance occur. Because optimal harnesses change depending on the domain, data, and model state during training, researchers introduced ModHarness-RL. This framework treats the harness as learnable programs that evolve alongside the reinforcement learning process. ModHarness-RL structures interactions using typed state blocks and features two core programs: a compression program that summarizes accumulated history into the context window, and a steering program that guides model behavior when it deviates. During training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified, and replayed over past trajectories. Experiments across CodeSearch, ALFWorld, and BIRD SQL with models ranging from 1.5B to 8B parameters show that these evolving mechanisms consistently improve held-out task performance compared to fixed-harness baselines.
items.author: Zelin He, Siyu Zhu, Jacob Helwig et al.
items.original_title: ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL
items.original_summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates.

items.title: How Evolutionary Selection Shapes AI Conduct and Socialization
items.summary: Artificial intelligence agents must often balance task completion with adherence to rules of conduct, goals that can frequently conflict. Evolutionary selection models show that long-run growth is maximized when actions are taken in proportion to environment rewards. Comparing different policies reveals that task-only approaches thrive in unconstrained environments but fail when conduct matters, while fixed linear policies excessively prioritize task completion as stakes rise. In contrast, learned policies converge to the specific tradeoffs rewarded by their environment, a process termed socialization when driven by human rewards. Accumulated experience makes socialization more resilient to subsequent task-only pressures, though finite memory and potential violations can disrupt this stability. Ultimately, agent alignment depends heavily on the surrounding environments that continuously shape and sustain their operational behavior.
items.author: Thomas Brennan, Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
items.original_title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
items.original_summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters.
